title: Single int Field
question: What is sizeof(A) on a 64-bit system (assuming standard alignment)?
explanation: An int is 4 bytes. No padding needed — the struct is exactly 4 bytes.

title: Two ints
question: What is sizeof(B)?
explanation: Two consecutive ints — 4 + 4 = 8 bytes. Both are naturally aligned, no padding required.

title: char then int (Padding!)
question: What is sizeof(C) due to alignment padding?
explanation: char a is 1 byte. int b requires 4-byte alignment, so 3 bytes of padding are inserted after a. Total: 1 + 3 + 4 = 8 bytes.

title: int, char, int (Sandwich Padding)
question: What is sizeof(D)?
layout: [ int a (4) | char b (1) | pad (3) | int c (4) ]
explanation: int a = 4, char b = 1, then 3 bytes of padding to align int c to a 4-byte boundary, int c = 4. Total: 4+1+3+4 = 12 bytes.

title: Two chars
question: What is sizeof(E)?
explanation: Both chars are 1 byte each with alignment 1 — no padding needed. Total: 2 bytes.

title: char, short, int
question: What is sizeof(F)?
layout: [ char a (1) | pad (1) | short b (2) | int c (4) ]
explanation: char a = 1. short requires 2-byte alignment → 1 byte padding. short b = 2. int requires 4-byte alignment (already aligned). int c = 4. Total: 1+1+2+4 = 8 bytes.

title: double then int (Tail Padding)
question: What is sizeof(G)?
explanation: double d = 8. int x = 4. The struct's alignment is max(8,4) = 8, so size must be a multiple of 8. 8+4 = 12, rounded up to 16. 4 bytes of tail padding added.

title: char then long long (Big Padding)
question: What is sizeof(H) on a 64-bit system?
layout: [ char a (1) | pad (7) | long long b (8) ]
explanation: char a = 1. long long requires 8-byte alignment → 7 bytes of padding. long long b = 8. Total: 1+7+8 = 16 bytes.

title: Array Field
question: What is sizeof(I)?
explanation: An int is 4 bytes, so int[3] = 3 × 4 = 12 bytes. Arrays have no extra padding between elements.

title: Union Size
question: What is sizeof(U)?
layout: [ all members overlap — size = largest member ]
explanation: A union's size equals its largest member. double c = 8 bytes is the largest. All members share the same memory location — sizeof(U) = 8.

title: Optimal Field Ordering
question: What are sizeof(Bad) and sizeof(Good) respectively?
layout:
Bad:  [ char a(1)|pad(3)|int b(4)|char c(1)|pad(3) ] = 12
Good: [ int b(4)|char a(1)|char c(1)|pad(2) ] = 8
explanation: Bad: char+pad+int+char+pad = 1+3+4+1+3 = 12. Good: int+char+char+pad = 4+1+1+2 = 8. Ordering fields largest-to-smallest reduces padding waste.

title: short, int, short
question: What is sizeof(J)?
layout: [ short a (2) | pad (2) | int b (4) | short c (2) | tail-pad (2) ]
explanation: short a = 2, pad = 2 (to align int to 4), int b = 4, short c = 2, tail-pad = 2 (struct must be a multiple of 4, its largest alignment). Total: 12 bytes.

title: Bit Fields
question: What is sizeof(K)? (all fields fit in one unsigned int)
layout: [ bits 0-3: a | bits 4-7: b | bits 8-31: c ] — all in 1 unsigned int
explanation: 4 + 4 + 24 = 32 bits — exactly one unsigned int. The compiler packs all bit fields into a single 4-byte unsigned int. sizeof(K) = 4.

title: Nested Struct
question: What is sizeof(Outer)?
explanation: char a = 1. Inner has alignment 4 (due to int y), so 3 bytes padding. Inner is 8 bytes (char+3pad+int). Total: 1+3+8 = 12 bytes.

title: Pointer Field Size
question: What is sizeof(P) on a 64-bit system?
explanation: On 64-bit, pointers are 8 bytes. char c = 1 byte. Struct alignment = 8 (largest member). Size must be multiple of 8: 8+1 = 9, rounded to 16. 7 bytes tail padding.
